Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Every Cauchy sequence of reals converges to a real ([[def-real-limit]]).

More carefully, this is a statement about the *axioms*: in a complete ordered
field, that is in an ordered field with the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), every Cauchy sequence converges. The proof
below uses nothing about $\mathbb{R}$ except that property, through
[[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]].

**This library already knows the conclusion by a different route.**
It is proved on the Cauchy-construction page, where
$\mathbb{R}$ is built out of Cauchy sequences of rationals and completeness is
read off the construction. That proof is about a particular construction; this
one is about the axioms, and it is what tells us the statement holds in *any*
complete ordered field, however it was obtained.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

derivations.claim: Write each component as a finite sum $F_i(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in E_i}c_{i\alpha}x^\alpha$. On any bounded coordinate box, for each exponent $q\ge1$ the identity $a^q-b^q=(a-b)\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}a^{q-1-j}b^j$ bounds the difference of each monomial at two points by a finite constant times their Euclidean distance; telescoping over the $N$ factors and summing the finitely many monomials proves that $F$ is locally Lipschitz there. It is also continuous, so [F1] applies at every state.

Put $R_+=\max(1,R)$ and $M_R=\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^N(\sum_{\alpha\in E_i}|c_{i\alpha}|R_+^{|\alpha|})^2\bigr)^{1/2}$. Since $|x_j(t)|\le R$ for each coordinate, the finite polynomial sums give $\|F(x(t))\|_2\le M_R$ for all $t<T_*$.

For $0\le s<t<T_*$, apply [F3] to $x|_{[s,t]}$ to obtain $\|x(t)-x(s)\|_2\le M_R(t-s)$. Thus, for $t_n=T_*(1-1/n)$, $n\ge2$, each coordinate sequence $(x_i(t_n))_{n\ge2}$ is Cauchy because $|x_i(t_n)-x_i(t_m)|\le\|x(t_n)-x(t_m)\|_2\le M_R|t_n-t_m|$. By [F2], each coordinate has a real limit $\xi_i$; set $x_*=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N)\in\mathbb R^N$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose for each of the finitely many coordinates an index after which $|x_i(t_n)-\xi_i|<\varepsilon/\sqrt N$, and take the maximum of those indices. Then $\|x(t_n)-x_*\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^N|x_i(t_n)-\xi_i|^2<\varepsilon^2$, so $x(t_n)\to x_*$. For any $t<T_*$ and all sufficiently large $n$ with $t_n\ge t$, the same Lipschitz bound gives $\|x(t)-x_*\|_2\le M_R(t_n-t)+\|x(t_n)-x_*\|_2$; letting $n\to\infty$ yields $\|x(t)-x_*\|_2\le M_R(T_*-t)$, so $x(t)\to x_*$. The closed-ball bound passes to the limit, hence $\|x_*\|_2\le R$.
By step 1.1 the polynomial field is locally Lipschitz near $x_*$. Apply [F1] to the IVP at $(T_*,x_*)$ to obtain a local solution $y$ on an open interval about $T_*$.

By [F4], $x(t)=x_0+\int_0^tF(x(s))\,ds$ for $t<T_*$ and $y(t)=x_*+\int_{T_*}^tF(y(s))\,ds$ near $T_*$. The limit in step 3.1 and continuity of $F$ extend the first identity to $t=T_*$. Define $\widetilde x=x$ before $T_*$ and $\widetilde x=y$ from $T_*$ onward, assigning the common value $x_*$ at $T_*$. The joined curve is continuous and the two integral identities add to its Volterra equation on $[0,T_*+\epsilon)$ for some $\epsilon>0$; [F4] therefore makes it a $C^1$ solution of the same ODE extending $x$.
The extension in step 5.1 agrees with the original curve at every $t<T_*$ and is defined beyond $T_*$. This proves the statement.

**Choice context.** The finite coefficient arrays and weighted coefficient completion below are defined without Countable Choice. In this coefficient-only reading, a finite real trigonometric polynomial is specified by a finite coefficient array $(a_k)$, extended by zero and satisfying $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$, and $\widehat q(k):=a_k$ denotes its specified coefficient coordinate. For the normalized Haar-measure conventions, integral Fourier coefficients and $L^2$ realization below, additionally assume Countable Choice, as in the declared measure and Fourier suppliers. In that analytic context the coefficient coordinates agree with the integral coefficients.

Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $N\ge1$ be integers. Let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ carry the probability measure obtained by pushing normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ forward under $y\mapsto x=2\pi y$; in coordinates this is $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For any componentwise integrable real $q:Q_d\to\mathbb R^N$, considered up to equality almost everywhere, and $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, define its componentwise Fourier coefficient by $\widehat q(k)=\int_{Q_d}q(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$; this integral is finite because $|e^{ik\cdot x}|=1$ and $q\in L^1$. A finite real trigonometric polynomial is a finite sum $q(x)=\sum_{k\in F}a_ke^{ik\cdot x}$, where $F\subset\mathbb Z^d$ is finite and the coefficients, extended by zero outside $F$, satisfy $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$. Such polynomials are integrable and satisfy $\widehat q(-k)=\overline{\widehat q(k)}$. Put $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$. For any $s\in\mathbb R$, define $H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ as the completion of finite real trigonometric polynomials in the norm $\|q\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat q(k)|^2$. Identify this completion with the weighted coefficient space subject to conjugate symmetry, using finite symmetric cutoffs, and write $\widehat q(k)$ for its coefficient coordinate. Under Countable Choice, if $s\ge0$, each element has a unique $L^2$ representative, and its coefficient coordinate agrees with the normalized integral formula; for $s<0$ no $L^2$ representative is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

abla q}(k)=ik\widehat q(k)$, and for tensor fields set $\widehat{\operatorname{div}F}_i(k)=i\sum_jk_j\widehat F_{ij}(k)$. These derivative maps are bounded from $H^s$ to $H^{s-1}$. The multipliers $P$ and $Q$ are real-preserving and bounded on every $H^s$, $s\in\mathbb R$; $P$ is an orthogonal projection and commutes with these derivatives. For every $F$ and every $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, their exact identity is the coefficientwise equality
$$\widehat{
abla QF}(k)=-(I-P_k)\widehat{\operatorname{div}F}(k).$$
In particular, both sides have zero coefficient at $k=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and use $H^\sigma(Q_d)$ with the normalized measure and weights in the Definition. For every integer $j\ge0$ and $\sigma>j+d/2$, each scalar $q\in H^\sigma(Q_d)$ has a $C^j$ representative and $\|q\|_{C^j}\le C_{d,\sigma,j}\|q\|_{H^\sigma}$. For every $\sigma>d/2$, pointwise multiplication extends uniquely from trigonometric polynomials to a continuous bilinear map $H^\sigma\times H^\sigma\to H^\sigma$ satisfying $\|fg\|_{H^\sigma}\le C_{d,\sigma}\|f\|_{H^\sigma}\|g\|_{H^\sigma}$. The assertions extend componentwise to finite-dimensional vector and tensor fields.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $m\ge s\ge4$ be integers, let $f,g\in C^\infty(Q_d;\mathbb R)$, and define $\Lambda^m$ by $\widehat{\Lambda^m q}(k)=w_k^m\widehat q(k)$. For each coordinate $j$,
$$\|[\Lambda^m,f]\partial_jg\|_{L^2}\le C_{d,m,s}\bigl(\|f\|_{H^m}\|g\|_{H^s}+\|f\|_{H^s}\|g\|_{H^m}\bigr),$$
where $[\Lambda^m,f]h=\Lambda^m(fh)-f\Lambda^mh$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $N\ge1$, let $F:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^N$ be a polynomial map, and let $T_*>0$. If $x\in C^1([0,T_*),\mathbb R^N)$ solves $x'(t)=F(x(t))$ and there is $R\ge0$ such that $\|x(t)\|_2\le R$ for every $0\le t<T_*$, then there are $\epsilon>0$ and a solution $\widetilde x\in C^1([0,T_*+\epsilon),\mathbb R^N)$ of the same ODE with $\widetilde x(t)=x(t)$ for $0\le t<T_*$. Thus a finite right endpoint of a bounded finite-dimensional polynomial ODE trajectory is extendible.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ have normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, write $|\alpha|=\sum_j\alpha_j$ and $\partial^\alpha=\partial_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots\partial_d^{\alpha_d}$. Give $C^\infty(Q_d;\mathbb R)$ the Fr'echet topology generated by $p_m(\phi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\|\partial^\alpha\phi\|_\infty$, for $m\in\mathbb N_0$, where the derivatives are those of the smooth periodic lift to $\mathbb R^d$. A periodic distribution is a continuous real-linear functional on this test space, extended complex-linearly to complex-valued tests. For such a distribution $S$, define $\widehat S(k)=\langle S,e^{-ik\cdot x}angle$ for $e_k(x)=e^{ik\cdot x}$ and define its mean to be $\widehat S(0)=\langle S,1angle$. For an integrable function $g$, the pairing is $\langle g,\phiangle=\int_{Q_d}g\phi\,d\mu$. Define distributional derivatives by $\langle\partial_jS,\phiangle=-\langle S,\partial_j\phiangle$. For a smooth scalar test, $
abla\phi=(\partial_1\phi,\ldots,\partial_d\phi)$ and $\Delta\phi=\sum_j\partial_j^2\phi$; for a smooth vector field $v$, $\operatorname{div}v=\sum_j\partial_jv_j$, $(v\otimes v)_{ij}=v_iv_j$, and $(v\cdot
abla)v_i=\sum_jv_j\partial_jv_i$. In particular, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ distributionally means $-\int_{Q_d}u\cdot
abla\phi\,d\mu=0$ for every real test function $\phi$. Equality of periodic distributions means equality on every such test function. Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $s>d/2+1$, and let $u\in H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $\operatorname{div}u=0$ in this sense. Then $u\otimes u\in H^s$, the mean-zero scalar $\pi=Q(u\otimes u)$ belongs to $H^s$, and in $H^{s-1}$,
$$P(u\cdot
abla u)=u\cdot
abla u+
abla\pi.$$
Among mean-zero periodic distributions $\widetilde\pi$ for which this identity holds as an equality of periodic distributions, this pressure is unique. The formula is a torus pressure recovery result and asserts no wall pressure regularity.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $T>0$, and $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For $z:Q_d\to\mathbb R^M$, use componentwise Fourier coefficients $\widehat z(k)=\int_{Q_d}z(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$, weights $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$, and the weighted coefficient completion norm $\|z\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat z(k)|^2$; the normalized Fourier isometry gives $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_k|\widehat z(k)|^2$, where $\|z\|_2=(\int_{Q_d}|z|^2\,d\mu)^{1/2}$ and the pointwise component norm is Euclidean. In particular, $H^0=L^2$. For a map $z:[0,T]\times Q_d\to\mathbb R^M$, smooth on the closed cylinder means that for every $m\in\mathbb N_0$ and spatial multi-index $\alpha$, $\partial_t^m\partial_x^\alpha z$ exists on $(0,T)\times Q_d$ and extends continuously to $[0,T]\times Q_d$; spatial derivatives are those of its periodic lift. For a spatial vector field define $\operatorname{div}z=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jz_j$ and $\Delta z=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_j^2z$. Write $\nabla z$ for the spatial Jacobian and $\|\nabla z(t)\|_\infty=\sup_{x\in Q_d}|\nabla z(t,x)|_F$, where $|\cdot|_F$ is the Euclidean Frobenius matrix norm. Let $P$ be the coefficientwise vector multiplier with $P_0=I$ and $P_k=I-kk^{\mathsf T}/|k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. The equations below hold pointwise on $(0,T)\times Q_d$ and at the time endpoints by continuous extension.

(i) If $\nu\ge0$ and $u,v\in C^\infty([0,T]\times Q_d;\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy, for each $z\in\{u,v\}$,
$$z_t+P((z\cdot\nabla)z)=\nu\Delta z,\qquad \operatorname{div}z=0,$$
then for every $t\in[0,T]$, with $w=u-v$,
$$\|w(t)\|_2^2\le\|w(0)\|_2^2\exp\!\left(2\int_0^t\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_\infty\,d\tau\right).$$

(ii) Let $N\ge1$ and, for $1\le j\le d$, let $A_j:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ be a fixed real-linear map whose image consists of symmetric matrices. If $q,r\in C^\infty([0,T]\times Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ satisfy, for each $z\in\{q,r\}$,
$$z_t+\sum_{j=1}^dA_j(z)\partial_jz=0,$$
then for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|q(t)-r(t)\|_2^2\le\|q(0)-r(0)\|_2^2\exp\!\left(C_{d,N,A}\int_0^t(\|\nabla q(\tau)\|_\infty+\|\nabla r(\tau)\|_\infty)\,d\tau\right),$$
where $C_{d,N,A}$ depends only on $d,N$ and the operator norms of the finitely many maps $A_j$. For either pair $(z_1,z_2)=(u,v)$ or $(q,r)$, put $w=z_1-z_2$. Let $\Gamma\ge0$ be any uniform rate for which the corresponding squared $L^2$ estimate above gives $\|w(t)\|_2^2\le\|w(0)\|_2^2e^{\Gamma t}$. If $s\ge1$ and $\max_{t\in[0,T]}\max(\|z_1(t)\|_{H^s},\|z_2(t)\|_{H^s})\le M$ for some $M\ge0$, define
$$B_s(M)=\begin{cases}1,&s=1,\\(2M)^{(s-1)/s},&s>1.\end{cases}$$
Then for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|w(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le B_s(M)\|w(0)\|_2^{1/s}e^{\Gamma t/(2s)}.$$
These are conditional estimates for already given smooth maps on the stated cylinder and assert no existence theorem. All quantities are mathematical and no physical units are assigned to $\nu$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The coefficient vector field is polynomial, hence locally Lipschitz by the finite-monomial estimate in the proof of [[lem-fd-polynomial-ode-continuation]]; [F6] gives a unique local real solution, and its right-hand side preserves $X_N$.

abla\Lambda^mu_N)\,dx= rac12\int u_N\cdot
abla|\Lambda^mu_N|^2\,dx=0$ by periodicity and $\operatorname{div}u_N=0$. The remaining commutator is bounded by [F5], while viscosity contributes $-
u\|
abla u_N\|_{H^m}^2$, giving $ rac12 rac d{dt}\|u_N\|_{H^m}^2+
u\|
abla u_N\|_{H^m}^2\le C_m\|u_N\|_{H^s}\|u_N\|_{H^m}^2$.

At $m=s$, set $Y_N=\|u_N\|_{H^s}$. When $Y_N>0$, the inequality in step 1.2 gives $Y_N'\le C_sY_N^2$; if $Y_N(0)=0$, uniqueness of the finite-dimensional ODE makes $u_N\equiv0$. Otherwise, integrating $(1/Y_N)'\ge-C_s$ shows $Y_N(t)\le2\|u_0\|_{H^s}$ for $0\le t\le T$, where $T=(2C_s\|u_0\|_{H^s})^{-1}$. For zero datum take $T=1$. These bounds do not use $\nu$ or higher norms.

Multiplying by $e^{-4C_m\|u_0\|_{H^s}t}$ and differentiating proves $\|u_N(t)\|_{H^m}\le\|u_0\|_{H^m}e^{2C_m\|u_0\|_{H^s}T}$ on the same interval. Parseval [F2] and the $H^s$ bound control the Euclidean coefficient norm of $u_N$; [F7] therefore extends each finite-dimensional solution through $[0,T]$, even though the constants $C_m$ may depend on $m$.

For every integer $m\ge s+2$, the product estimate [F4] and the bounds in step 3.1 give a uniform bound on $\partial_tu_N=-S_NP(u_N\cdot\nabla u_N)+\nu\Delta u_N$ in $C([0,T],H^{m-2})$. Thus each fixed Fourier coefficient is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous in time.

Fix lengths $L_1,L_2>0$ and width $h>0$. Define the periodic channel
$$\Omega_{\mathrm{per}}=(\mathbb R/L_1\mathbb Z)\times(0,h)\times(\mathbb R/L_2\mathbb Z)$$
and the infinite channel
$$\Omega_{\infty}=\mathbb R\times(0,h)\times\mathbb R.$$
Both have the product Euclidean metric. On $\Omega_{\mathrm{per}}$, the first and third coordinates are periodic quotient coordinates with periods $L_1$ and $L_2$; differential operators are the ordinary coordinate operators applied to periodic lifts. On $\Omega_{\infty}$, all three coordinates are ordinary real coordinates. The closures add the two wall faces at $y=0$ and $y=h$, and no other spatial boundary is imposed. A vector field is $C^\infty$ up to these walls when it is smooth in the interior and every spatial derivative of every order extends continuously to both faces on each compact coordinate patch. Its homogeneous no-slip boundary condition is $u=0$ on the two wall faces; prescribed wall velocity $g$ means the trace condition $u=g$. The definition imposes no decay or other condition at infinity on $\Omega_{\infty}$; such conditions must be stated separately.

By the coordinate formula for curl, $\nabla\times(U(y),0,0)=(0,0,-U'(y))=(0,0,-V/h)$. The flux is $\int_0^hVy/h\,dy=Vh/2$.
